description: Compare two conflict-free LR(1) states that share a core and see how taking their union in LALR(1) creates reduce-reduce conflicts on both lookaheads.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Lines 2-3 represent two LR(1) states as sets of `(lhs, rhs, dot, lookahead)` 4-tuples. After reading `a c`, `A -> c .` has lookahead `'d'` and `B -> c .` has lookahead `'e'`. After `b c`, those two lookaheads are swapped. `core(state)` strips the fourth element (`lookahead`) to return the underlying LR(0) items.

`reduce_conflicts(state)` checks every completed item (`dot == len(rhs.split())` on line 11). It groups reductions by their lookahead token in `wants`. It returns any lookahead token that maps to more than one production.
Lines 15-16 check `STATE_AFTER_A_C` and `STATE_AFTER_B_C` separately and print `conflicts none` for each, because within each individual LR(1) state `'d'` and `'e'` point to different reductions.

steps.answer: Both `A -> c` and `B -> c` now carry lookaheads `'d'` and `'e'` in `merged`. Thus, `reduce_conflicts(merged)` returns `{'d': ['A -> c', 'B -> c'], 'e': ['A -> c', 'B -> c']}`.
steps.question: When line 19 merges the two states with `merged = STATE_AFTER_A_C | STATE_AFTER_B_C`, what dictionary does `reduce_conflicts(merged)` return on line 20?

steps.description: Line 18 confirms `core(STATE_AFTER_A_C) == core(STATE_AFTER_B_C)` is `True`, and lines 19-20 take the set union `merged` and print the two reduce-reduce conflicts on `'d'` and `'e'`.
On line 19, `merged` combines all four items into a single 4-element set before `reduce_conflicts(merged)` detects the collisions.

title: How LALR(1) State Merging Can Introduce a Reduce-Reduce Conflict
